blocks.text: I can use reflexive pronouns ‘me’ and ‘te’ to describe my daily routine and ask you questions about yours.
Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: used to indicate doing something to yourself, words like ‘myself’ and ‘yourself’

blocks.text: Here are some verbs that the López family use to talk about routines. Each one is an infinitive.

blocks.q: Match each Spanish verb to its English meaning.

blocks.text: With regular -ar verbs, the ‘I’ form ends in **-o** and the ‘you’ form ends in **-as**. Remove the -ar, then add the ending.
To say that **I** do something to **myself**, add the reflexive pronoun **me**.

items: Presento a mi amigo. (I introduce my friend.)

blocks.text: The reflexive pronoun goes {before} the verb in Spanish, but after it in English. The verb ending is still -o.

blocks.label: Me llamo … or llamo …?
blocks.text: ‘Me llamo …’ means ‘I call myself …’. A more natural translation is ‘I’m called …’ or ‘My name is …’. ‘Llamo …’ means ‘I call (someone else)’.
To say that **you** do something to **yourself**, add the reflexive pronoun **te** before the verb.

items: Despiertas a tu hermano. (You wake your brother up.)

blocks.text: The verb ending is still {-as}. The infinitive ‘lavar’ just means ‘to wash’: you need a reflexive pronoun to mean ‘wash yourself’.

blocks.label: Watch out!
blocks.text: In English, we often drop the reflexive pronoun, but it is always needed in Spanish.
Some verbs, like **despertar**, have a stem change from -e to -ie in some forms.

blocks.label: How do I say ‘I wake up’?
blocks.text: Me despierto. The reflexive pronoun ‘me’ goes before the verb, and the verb has the spelling change: despierto.
The verb **poner** has an irregular ‘I’ form: **pongo**. The other present tense forms are regular. Used reflexively, poner means to put clothing on.

items: Me pongo un vestido. (I put a dress on.)
Te pones el reloj. (You put your watch on.)

blocks.text: In English, we usually say ‘my’ or ‘your’ before the noun. In Spanish, just use {el} or {la}.

slides.title: Routine verbs with me and te

blocks.text: ‘Me preparo’ is literally ‘I prepare myself’. But **desayunar** is never used with reflexive pronouns: ‘I have breakfast’ is just **desayuno**.

slides.title: me and te, or mi and tu?

blocks.text: **Me** and **te** look very like **mi** and **tu**, but we use them differently.

items: {Me} (myself) is followed by a verb: Me lavo. (I wash (myself).)
{Mi} (my) is usually followed by a noun: Mi libro es nuevo. (My book is new.)
{Te} (yourself) is followed by a verb: Te levantas. (You get (yourself) up.)
{Tu} (your) is usually followed by a noun: Tu móvil es rojo. (Your phone is red.)

blocks.text: Take care not to pronounce Spanish **me** like English ‘me’: that is the same sound as Spanish **mi**, and could confuse things!
Look at the word after the gap. Is it a verb or a noun?

blocks.q: Choose the correct word to complete each sentence.

items.q: Hoy ___ levanto temprano. (Today I get up early.)
___ móvil está encima de la mesa. (My phone is on top of the table.)
¿Por qué no ___ lavas ahora? (Why don’t you wash now?)
Daniel, ___ preparas para el colegio. (Daniel, you get ready for school.)

blocks.q: How do you say ‘I put my watch on’?
blocks.why: With poner used reflexively, Spanish uses el or la (not mi or tu) before the clothing, and the reflexive pronoun me goes before the verb.
Desayunar means to have breakfast, and the ‘you’ form ends in -as. No reflexive pronoun is used.

items: The ‘I’ form of regular -ar verbs like lavar ends in -o. The ‘you’ form ends in -as.
Some verbs like despertar have a stem change from -e to -ie in some forms, e.g. despierto (I wake up).
To say that I do something to myself, use me before the verb: me presento (I introduce myself).
To say that you do something to yourself, use te before the verb: te llamas (you call yourself).
Me and te look like mi and tu, but they are different: me and te are followed by a verb; mi and tu are usually followed by a noun.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Routine events: reflexive pronouns ‘me’ and ‘te’
worksheet.instructions: Answer each question with a short answer. Some answers are in Spanish and some are in English. Remember: me and te go before a verb; mi and tu go before a noun.

questions.prompt: Complete with me or mi: ___ lavo más tarde. (I wash later.)
questions.explanation: Lavo is a verb, so we need the reflexive pronoun me.

questions.prompt: Complete with me or mi: ___ reloj dice que son las ocho. (My watch says it is eight o’clock.)
questions.explanation: Reloj is a noun, so we need the possessive adjective mi.

questions.prompt: Complete with me or mi: ___ hermano está en la cocina. (My brother is in the kitchen.)
questions.explanation: Hermano is a noun, so we need mi.

questions.prompt: Complete with me or mi: ___ preparo para el colegio. (I get ready for school.)
questions.explanation: Preparo is a verb, so we need me.
Tu is ‘your’ before a singular noun, and hijo is son.
Mi is ‘my’ before a singular noun, and ordenador is computer.

questions.prompt: Write in Spanish: “do you get up?” (use the ‘you’ form with the reflexive pronoun)
questions.explanation: Te goes before the verb, and the ‘you’ form of levantar ends in -as.
Te preparas is the ‘you’ form of preparar used reflexively, meaning ‘you get ready’.

questions.prompt: Write in Spanish: “I put on” (clothes), using the reflexive pronoun and the ‘I’ form of poner.
questions.explanation: Me goes before the verb, and the ‘I’ form of poner is pongo.
Me goes before the verb, and the ‘I’ form of preparar ends in -o.

questions.prompt: One of these verbs is never used with reflexive pronouns: llamar, desayunar, lavar. Which one?
questions.explanation: Desayunar is never used with reflexive pronouns: desayuno means ‘I have breakfast’.
